lever: ">150k context" (main-session context size versus the repo's recycle thresholds, which are percentages of a 1M window)
headline: Main sessions run on 1M windows with a median per-request context of 231k (p90 459k, p99 649k, max 774k), measured. The recycle rails only act at 25-75% of 1M (250k-750k), so 89% of main-session input-side tokens are sent above 150k and 54% above 300k. In the simulation, recycling every main session at 250k with a measured 100k re-prime cuts main-session input-side tokens by about 37% raw, 8.2B of 22.4B per week. At the price-ratio weighting, which matches /usage closely, that is 32%, or about 14.5% of all usage across the 4 accounts. Recycling at 150k saves more on paper, 38-51% weighted, but it would force about 2,000 recycles a week, roughly 2.5 per session. Those figures are estimates.

recommendations.action: Shrink the 60k first-request baseline (system prompt, CLAUDE.md, rules, tools, hook injections). Every recycle pays it again as a cache write, so a smaller baseline makes lower thresholds cheaper. Measure it with cc-ctx-audit before cutting.

caveats: The weighting is an assumption. I used uncached input 1, cache read 0.1, cache write 1.25, output 5 because it reproduces /usage's '>150k' shares to within 0.2 points. Other weightings fit almost as well (0.15/2.0 gives 0.4), and Anthropic does not publish how Max-plan limits weight cache reads. Raw unweighted figures are given alongside.

The simulation assumes the work after a recycle produces the same per-request context growth as the original session. The successor's state rebuild is approximated only by its starting size R (60k or 100k) plus 3 handoff requests at T charged as cache reads. Lost context that forces extra re-reads, extra requests, and any quality or rework effects are not modelled, so the savings are upper-bound estimates.

Main and subagent records were separated by path (/subagents/) and by isSidechain. Subagents use 55% of all weighted usage and 49% of their tokens sit above 150k, but the session recycle rails do not govern them, so they are outside this lever.

A transcript file was used as a proxy for a session. 11 of 785 'fresh' first requests were above 150k, which are probably resumes or forks; they were left in the R distribution. Sessions whose first request fell before the 7-day cutoff were not counted as fresh.
The fresh-session p50 of 60k is an observed baseline. I did not break down what it contains; cc-ctx-audit and cc-quota-price --census were not run.
I did not fetch the X post the operator linked. The computed brief asked only for this measurement, so this result does not judge whether that prompt helps.
All scripts and the request CSV are in /tmp/usage-audit/: scan.py, analyze.py, sim.py, sim2.py, xcheck.py, fit.py, requests.csv. Nothing was written anywhere else, and nothing in the repo was edited.

caveats: The brief says the current binary is /opt/homebrew/bin/claude 2.1.291. The launcher pin (cc-claude-bin, ~/.zshrc _bin=) and the 28 live sessions use ~/.claude-293 at 2.1.293, and I ran my timed JSON check with that binary.

The .result field of the JSON output is human prose, not structured data. Anthropic calls it 'Approximate' and its percentages 'independent characteristics, not a breakdown'; how they are weighted is not documented. A parser for it can break on any Claude Code update, so the wrapper must store the raw text and abstain when parsing fails.

The breakdown covers local transcripts for each config dir only. ~/.claude-next/projects is a symlink to ~/.claude/projects, so the 'next' figures include stable-track sessions. Account transplants copy sessions between dirs (cc-token-ledger notes 8% of responses are transplant duplicates), so per-account shares may double-count. I did not measure that for /usage.

I tested --safe-mode and --no-session-persistence on one account only (next3). I did not reproduce the quaternary 'workspace untrusted, 37 allow rules ignored' warning (it is not in the saved /tmp/usage-audit/next4.txt). /usage runs no tools, so the ignored allow rules should not matter, but that is unverified.

Side effects of the earlier collection, already done and not undone: 6 transcripts of about 14 KB from 2.1.291 /usage runs plus 2 from 2.0.5, written under the four config dirs' project folders for this worktree; SessionStart hook chains fired; one run added to the stray ~/.claude-next4. I deleted nothing. Whether to remove ~/.claude-next4 is the operator's decision.

Timings were taken at load average 133 (uptime), with other workers writing to /tmp/usage-audit at the same time. My own files are only /tmp/usage-audit/w-usage-src/*, /tmp/usage-audit/inspect_usage_tx.py, /tmp/usage-audit/bare_claude_scan.py, /tmp/usage-audit/bare_claude_scan2.py and /tmp/usage-audit/bare-claude-hits.txt.

The bare-claude scan is a heuristic over command positions (tests, fixtures and vendor excluded) followed by manual review of each hit. A `claude` built dynamically, e.g. inside eval or from a variable holding the literal name, could be missed.

On the user's wider question: /usage confirms what our instruments already show. Most usage is in subagent-heavy, long-running sessions above 150k context. The genuinely new signals are the parallelism and top-skill shares. As a data source it adds monitoring, not savings.

The realistic ceiling is the timeout wakes: about 1.0% of meter weight (1.8% on the proxy). The subagent part of the estimate does not exist: those subagents are asynchronous workflow agents, and only 8 of 1,450 watcher turns launched any agent. The timeout wake is designed behaviour: cc-await-ping's C5 rule makes it 'the re-look at the world floor and the in-session deadline check for a peer that will never ping'. The file the recommendation names, hooks/mailbox-wake-arm.sh, already wakes only on mail and re-arms at Stop with no model turn. The wakes come from model-launched run_in_background cc-await-ping calls. The safe partial change is a longer timeout.

Dropping those turns entirely would save at most 2.44% proxy / 0.80% meter; dropping only the per-wake first request saves 1.14% / 0.34% (measured: batch.txt). Machine-triggered main-thread turns are 22% of meter weight, not 53%; the larger figure credits asynchronous workflow subagents to unrelated wakes. Idle loops are negligible (0.03%), and parallel sessions cost about the same per request. The 250k context cap is a lever the repo has already refuted, and it would be net negative. Fixing watcher timeouts is worth about 1% and batching peer messages under 1%. Removing watcher timeouts outright would cost the designed deadline-check function.

A lint must allow an explicit default type, because 10-28% of the traffic legitimately needs it. Also, workflow-lean omits the project CLAUDE.md, so review:* slots lose the project rules unless they read them on demand, which the lean contract tells them to do.

Rec 2 (turn off or name-only the 13 zero-use visual and niche skills, a claimed 0.35B a week): refuted. corrected_headline: Measured over the last 7 days, with cross-account copies removed: a default workflow-subagent slot's first request is 47.6k tokens at the median, against 9.2k for workflow-lean. The difference is about 38.4k tokens of fixed overhead, re-read on every turn. All cache writes are 5-minute writes, and 88% of a default slot's first request is a fresh cache write, so the 1.25x weighting holds. Moving the eligible default slots to lean would have saved about 271M weighted tokens last week. That set is 1,759 slots and leaves out B13 rehearsal slots, whose briefs need git checkouts in sandboxes. The saving is 5.2% of the 5,207M total across the 4 accounts, and 4.7% to 6.6% under other cache weightings. This is last week's figure, not a guaranteed weekly one. About 124M of it came from the B13 agentsync loop, and open decision e869fac7eb34 proposes ending that loop after round 26. If it ends, the recurring saving is about 147M a week (2.8%), from ad-hoc workflows that set no agentType. /usage's per-account numbers include transcripts copied in from other accounts.
